topic: The Fractal Path: Ternary Logic and the Constrained Towers of Hanoi
target_audience: University students (Computer Science/Mathematics) or advanced high school students

sections.title: Introduction: The Restricted Puzzle
sections.content: Introduce the standard Towers of Hanoi but add a 'linear' constraint: disks can only move between adjacent pegs (A ↔ B and B ↔ C). A jump from A to C is forbidden. This restriction transforms a simple puzzle into a complex journey.
sections.example: A curious robot named 'Tertio' is trying to move 3 disks from Peg A to Peg C, but its mechanical arm is stuck—it can only shift disks to the peg immediately to its left or right.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Base-3 (Ternary) Counting
sections.content: Explain ternary counting (Base-3) where digits are 0, 1, and 2. Use a visual 'odometer' representation to show how numbers increment. Emphasize that while binary (Base-2) represents a 'yes/no' state, ternary represents 'left/middle/right' positions.
sections.example: Visualizing the number 13 in ternary: 111 (1*9 + 1*3 + 1*1). In our puzzle, each digit represents the peg location (0=A, 1=B, 2=C) of a specific disk.

sections.title: Mapping States to Ternary Coordinates
sections.content: Assign every possible configuration of the puzzle to a ternary number. For N disks, there are 3^N possible states. The largest disk is the most significant digit, and the smallest disk is the least significant digit.
sections.example: With 2 disks, state '02' means the large disk is on Peg A (0) and the small disk is on Peg C (2). This creates a unique 'address' for every possible layout of the game.

sections.title: The Geometry of Moves: The Sierpinski Gasket
sections.content: Visualize the state space as a graph. Each valid move between states is an edge. Because of the linear constraint, the state-transition graph forms a perfect Sierpinski Triangle (fractal). Moving one disk corresponds to moving along an edge of the triangle.
sections.example: An animation shows that for 1 disk, the graph is a line (A-B-C). For 2 disks, it becomes three connected lines forming a triangle. For 3 disks, it becomes the classic Sierpinski Gasket with 27 vertices.

sections.title: Graph Traversal: Finding the Optimal Path
sections.content: Explain that solving the puzzle is equivalent to traversing the 'outer edge' of the Sierpinski triangle. To get from state 000 (all on Peg A) to 222 (all on Peg C), the robot must visit every single node on the perimeter of the fractal.
sections.example: Trace a glowing line following the perimeter of the Sierpinski triangle. The sequence of nodes visited matches the sequence of ternary numbers if we follow a 'Gray Code' style path for the constrained puzzle.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Beauty of Mathematical Convergence
sections.content: Summarize how ternary counting (number theory), the Towers of Hanoi (algorithms), and the Sierpinski Triangle (fractal geometry) are actually three different ways of looking at the same underlying structure.
sections.example: Zoom out from the small 3-disk triangle to a massive 10-disk Sierpinski fractal, showing how the robot's simple rules create a complex, infinite geometric pattern.
